title: Allocating on heap and then use shared pointer, how to free the data
body_html:
I have the following scenario. I have a allocated a chunk of data using new, then assigned the block of data to a smart pointer in the class DNA_ImageBlob, how do I free T*blob data ?

template <class T>
void DNA_ImageBlob<T>::Reset(int h, int w, int c)
{
    SetWidth(w);
    SetHeight(h);
    SetDepth(c);
    T *blob = alocData(h, w, c);
    data_ = std::make_shared<T>(blob);
    compressed_ = false;
}

template <class T>
T *DNA_ImageBlob<T>::alocData(unsigned int h, unsigned int w, unsigned int d)
{
    if (w * h * d == 0)
    {
        return nullptr;
    }
    T *blob = new T[w * h * d];
    return blob;
}

events.body_html: You don't. The smart pointer does it for you. That's the whole point of using smart pointers.
Does this answer your question? How to use a custom deleter with a shared pointer
@VLL How is that answer related to my piece of code, can you explain more?

Do you really need a shared_ptr though? I would keep one blob per data item, make the data a std::vector and let RAII take care of the rest. Then you can just return a const& to the vector data if client code needs access. So DNA_Image blob is not a class used to allocate data, it really will represent a blob of data

en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/raii, try to understand this concept it is core of writing resource/memory leak free C++. And works great when you leave scopes of functions at multiple places (or use exceptions)
@PepijnKramer can you answer with pseudo code please ? That's what I really want to do, but I'm a beginner :)

If you want to use a shared pointer, you must use a custom deleter. That's because std::shared_ptr doesn't have an "array" overload, so it only does plain delete when you need delete[]. Mismatching news and deletes leads to undefined behavior.
And to emphasize the point of @PepijnKramer, do you really need a shared pointer? Do you even need new[] and delete[] and pointers? Why not use a std::vector<T>?
@Someprogrammerdude Can you elabratoe an answer with a custom deleter ?

Here is an example, if you have questions just ask.

#include <vector> 
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

// Blob is a RAII class, meaning its destructor will 
// cleanup all resources it owns (in this case memory held by vector)
class Blob
{
public:
    Blob(std::size_t width, std::size_t depth, std::size_t height) :
        m_blob_data(width * depth * height, 0) // allocates memory and sets it to 0. (last parameter is optional)
    {
    }

    // provide read only access to data
    const auto& get_data() const noexcept
    {
        return m_blob_data;
    }

    ~Blob() = default; 

private:
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> m_blob_data; // when destructor is called, vector gets destructed which will free memory
};

int main()
{
    // start a scope (yes this has meaning in C++, and is important with respect to RAII)
    {
        Blob blob{ 2,2,2 };
        std::cout << blob.get_data().size() << "\n"; // 2*2*2 = 8 items.
    } // blob goes out of scope here, so from here on memory is freed.

    return 0;
}

RAII guideline, avoid-new-and-delete-outside-resource-management-functions. In general avoid the use of new/delete, look for containers from the standard library, or use std::make_unique (std::shared_ptr has its own issues with respect to circular references, so must designed up front )

In modern C++ (>=03), if you need a list-like container your first choice should be std::vector<>. It's also your second and third. The only reason to be allocating arrays is a narrow set of compatibility use cases.
How can I replace alocData() with your own version ?

Not directly this is a different concept, it will not require alocData at all. The client that called allocData should now use get_data(). Just make sure your Blob lives long enough and isn't deleted before the caller is done with the data. Maybe you just need to learn a bit more C++? Here is a bit more on RAII, learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/destructors but I think it won't hurt you to go over the full course.

But this is something you have to figure out on your own.  (probably Blob needs to be templated too, so it can hold other things then a std::uint8_t). (Otherwise there is still unique_pointer and move, but that's a whole different story)
Do you think replacing shared_ptr, to unique ptr is a better approach

As said it all depends on the overall design what is best. A unique_ptr models the fact that there is only one owner at a time for the data. As said it is best if you learn a bit more about those concepts (like ownership). Then update your design with this lifecycles and ownserships in mind and ony then start refactoring. For now just put the delete in the correct place. What I mostly wanted to show you that "C++", standard library containers, RAII have their nicely interlocking way of doing things that can avoid a lot of (memory related) bugs

What do you mean by just put delete in the correct place?

There is code that calls allocate_data() which returns a T*, the calling code will need to delete this. Replacing that line with a std::make_unique and returning a unique_ptr might be the quickest fix. And that's what I will leave you with.
std::unique_ptr<T> blob = std::make_unique<T>[w * h * d]; is that what you mean ? The syntax is wrong :(
@AhmedSaleh auto blob = std::make_unique<T[]>(w * h * d);

Yes the latter one you are making an instance of an array of T, not a single one. The distinction is important. When the unique_ptr goes out of scope it will delete the memory for you (using a delete[] call)
